Figures describe the article as it stood on 2026-10-31 (that exact version). Computed 2026-11-03. Full data (JSON).

How the opening has changed

The whole first paragraph on 2015-01-01, 2019-01-01, 2023-01-01 and in the version analysed here (2026-10-31), as each read. Press Play on a version to watch the one before it turn into it: words taken out fade in red, words added appear in green. Above each, the short description: the line Wikipedia shows under the title in its search box and apps. Until about 2018 that line came from Wikidata, not from the article, so older versions often show none here. Under every paragraph, short description changes: each change to that line made since the column before (Play steps the line through them, with their dates, while the paragraph changes) (checked through the page history from 2017, when articles began to set it themselves; how); changes put back within a day are folded. Sources cited opens, under every column, the footnotes placed inside that first paragraph, read the same way as the article's, with today's ratings; many first paragraphs cite nothing, because Wikipedia's guideline lets the opening rest on sources cited further down (the whole article's sources at each date are under Sources cited). Sentences that changed most opens three rows: today's three most-changed opening sentences, each traced back through every date (at each, the opening sentence with most words in common, by a fixed rule), and through the two template columns; Play on a sentence shows its change from the column before. How this is compared.

1 January 2015
84 words, 4 sentences
Short description: none

Hezbollah (pronounced ; , literally "Party of Allah" or "Party of God")—also transliterated Hizbullah, Hizballah, etc.—is a Shi'a Islamist militant group and political party based in Lebanon. Hezbollah's paramilitary wing is the Jihad Council. After the death of Abbas al-Musawi in 1992, the organisation has been headed by Hassan Nasrallah, its Secretary-General. The United States, France, the Gulf Cooperation Council, United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, the Netherlands, the European Union and Israel classify Hezbollah as a terrorist organization, in whole or in part.

1 January 2023
52 words, 2 sentences
Short description: Lebanese Shia Islamist political party and militant group

Hezbollah (; , , also transliterated Hizbullah or Hizballah, among others) is a Lebanese Shia Islamist political party and militant group, led by its Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah since 1992. Hezbollah's paramilitary wing is the Jihad Council, and its political wing is the Loyalty to the Resistance Bloc party in the Lebanese Parliament.

Analysed version
72 words, 4 sentences
Short description: Islamist movement and militant group based in Lebanon

Hezbollah is a Lebanese Shia Islamist political party with an active paramilitary wing. Its military and security activities have been prohibited by the Lebanese government since March 2026, amid the 2026 Lebanon war. Hezbollah's paramilitary wing is the Jihad Council, and its political wing is the Loyalty to the Resistance Bloc party in the Lebanese Parliament. Its armed strength was assessed to be equivalent to that of a medium-sized army in 2016.

Hezbollah is a Lebanese Shia Islamist political party with an active paramilitary wing. According to Jamail, Hezbollah (; , , also transliterated Hizbullah or Hizballah, among others) is a Lebanese Shia Islamist political party and militant group, led by its Secretary-General Hassan Nasrallah since 1992. According to RT, Hezbollah (pronounced ; , literally "Party of Allah" or "Party of God")—also transliterated Hizbullah, Hizballah, etc.—is a Shi'a Islamist militant group and political party based in Lebanon. Its military and security activities have been prohibited by the Lebanese government since March 2026, amid the 2026 Lebanon war. Hezbollah's paramilitary wing is the Jihad Council, and its political wing is the Loyalty to the Resistance Bloc party in the Lebanese Parliament. According to World Policy Institute, Hezbollah's status as a legitimate political party, a terrorist group, a resistance movement, or some combination thereof is a contentious issue. Its armed strength was assessed to be equivalent to that of a medium-sized army in 2016. According to Benjamin, Gordon, Jodi and 1 others, the United States, France, the Gulf Cooperation Council, United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, the Netherlands, the European Union and Israel classify Hezbollah as a terrorist organization, in whole or in part.

According to RT, Hezbollah (pronounced ; , literally "Party of Allah" or "Party of God")—also transliterated Hizbullah, Hizballah, etc.—is a Shi'a Islamist militant group and political party based in Lebanon.

Wikipedia's voice in the opening

Each sentence of the opening section checked against Wikipedia's neutrality policy. A sentence is marked (orange edge) when there is evidence it is contested (editors took it out for a day or more and put it back, tagged it as disputed, or argued over it on the talk page; or it uses a word from Wikipedia's own “Words to watch” guideline) and it is stated in Wikipedia's voice, naming no one who holds the view. That marks sentences to check against the rule, not a finding that a sentence breaks it. “With attribution” names the cited authors in front of the sentence by a fixed template; the last column shows the earlier wording of the same sentence as Wikipedia printed it on 1 January of 2015, 2019, 2023, with the works it cited then that are gone now. Nothing here is written by this project, and it proposes no edit to Wikipedia (how).

How the summary rows are calculated. For the sources in scope that have a score s (independent quality, 0 to 1; or audience leaning, −1 to +1), each cited c times: mean per source = (s1 + … + sn) ÷ n, each source counted once; mean per citation = (c1·s1 + … + cn·sn) ÷ (c1 + … + cn), each source counted as often as it is cited. Both cover only scored sources: the share of citations they cover is given beside them. The rows cover every citation in scope, not only the sources listed in the table.

Opinion and harder-to-check citations

Of the article's 605 citations: opinion, comment or blog section 8 (1%) · no web link 66 (11%) · book with no page number 7 (1%) · not in English 12 (2%) · not in English, with no quote or translation 12 (2%) · behind a paywall or registration 8 (1%). We spot opinion pieces from the web address (such as /opinion/ or a blog) or from the footnote's own label. A book counts as not in English when the footnote says so, or when Open Library lists the book only in other languages. No quote or translation means the footnote does not copy out the passage it relies on, so a reader who does not know the language cannot check it. Each of these makes a footnote harder to check, not wrong.

About the ratings: Wikipedia's own list (Perennial sources) rates about 530 sources that its editors argue about often. Most sources are not on it; that is not a bad mark.
  • The quality score (Lin and colleagues, 2023) runs from 0 to 1 and covers news websites. Books and journals have no score.
  • Audience leaning says who shares a website, not what it publishes: −1 means only Democrats shared it, +1 only Republicans, 0 both equally. Out of every 100 people sharing it, Republicans = (1 + score) ÷ 2 × 100, so −0.4 is about 70 Democrats to 30 Republicans. It comes from US Twitter users matched to voter records (DomainDemo, 2025; Robertson and colleagues, 2018) and covers only websites shared widely enough.
  • Few publishers have a recorded political affiliation, and those records are written by volunteers on Wikidata and Wikipedia.
  • The ratings are today's ratings, not the ratings when the footnote was added.
  • Links between organisations (owner, founder, member of) come from Wikidata, which anyone can edit. † marks a fact for which Wikidata gives no source.
